items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Russian man accused of spying on US tech defence company that assists Ukraine
items.content:
Russian arrested for spying on US defence company Palantir over Ukraine support

11 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

The alleged foreign agent was discovered with two Russian passports

A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supports the Ukrainian military.

Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a covert operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. The BBC understands that the company targeted was Palantir Technologies.

D'iu is also charged with stalking employees and possessing falsified identity documents.

The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia.

"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.

"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."

Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.

He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".

On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.

He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.

His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".

The suspect allegedly took photos of employees screens at a cafe near the office

A source in the industry confirmed that Palantir was targeted, and added that the operation did not penetrate the company's private systems.

They added that the company has been "targeted extensively" by Russia over its involvement in Ukraine, and that the attacks are becoming "increasingly aggressive".

The source, who did not want to be named, said that this was the first time a Russian operative was found while on US soil attempting to spy on the company.

"I think the surprising thing is that they decided to take the risk of sending someone to the US," they said, in an attempt to get into the system "physically".

Palantir has not issued a statement in reaction to the charges.

D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.

On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.

During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".

A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.

He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.

items.title: Postgres is All You Need for Durable Workflows
items.content:
Durable workflows are a simple but powerful tool for building reliable programs. The idea is that as your program

runs, you regularly checkpoint its progress to a database. That way, if your program ever crashes or fails, you can

reload from the last checkpoint to recover it from its last completed step. You can think of this like saving in a

video game: you regularly “save” your program’s progress so that if it crashes, you can “reload” it from its last

Most commonly, durable workflows are implemented via external orchestration . This is the pattern used

by systems like Temporal, Airflow, and AWS Step Functions. In this model, durable programs are written as workflows of

steps whose execution is coordinated by a central orchestrator.

When a client submits a workflow, the orchestrator creates a record for it in a data store then dispatches it to a

worker for execution. Each time a worker completes a step, it sends the step’s outcome back to the orchestrator. The

orchestrator checkpoints the output in its data store, then dispatches the next step. If a worker crashes or fails,

the orchestrator dispatches its workflows to another worker, starting them from their last checkpointed step.

In this blog post, we’ll argue that external orchestration is fundamentally overcomplicated . The core

idea of durable workflows is to checkpoint program state in a database. But if durable workflows are about databases,

then there’s no reason to have a separate orchestrator server. Instead, it’s simpler and more efficient to use the

database itself as an orchestrator. To make this more concrete, we’ll focus specifically on building durable workflows

on Postgres, because its popularity, scalability , and rich ecosystem make it

In a Postgres-backed durable workflows system, application servers directly communicate with Postgres to execute

workflows instead of going through a central orchestrator. A client submits a workflow for execution by creating an

entry for it in a Postgres workflows table. Application servers poll the table for workflows to dequeue and execute.

As a server executes a workflow, it checkpoints the output of each step to Postgres. If a server executing workflows

crashes or fails, another server can recover its workflows from their checkpoints.

This design renders a central orchestrator unnecessary because application servers can coordinate through Postgres.

Instead of relying on a central orchestrator to dispatch workflows to workers, servers cooperatively dequeue workflows

from a Postgres table, using mechanisms such as locking clauses to ensure each workflow is dequeued by exactly one

worker. Instead of relying on an orchestrator to checkpoint step outputs, workers checkpoint steps to Postgres

themselves. If multiple workers try to execute the same workflow simultaneously, Postgres database integrity

constraints let them detect the duplicate work on checkpoint and back off.

Replacing a central orchestrator with Postgres (or another database) makes durable workflows fundamentally simpler. In

particular, it means hard problems such as scalability, availability, observability, and security can be addressed

using well-understood Postgres-native solutions.

The scalability and availability of a database-backed durable workflows system are fundamentally determined by the

underlying database. The system can scale horizontally by adding more worker servers, so its maximum capacity is

determined by how quickly the database can process workflows. Similarly, workers are fungible and can freely recover

each other’s state, so the system is available as long as the underlying database is available.

When using Postgres specifically, this is beneficial because Postgres scalability and availability are well-studied

problems with robust solutions. For scalability, a single Postgres server can vertically scale to handle

tens of thousands of workflows per second .

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future.

The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.

From the rollout of new lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the company. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.”

“We cannot continue to do the same things because the marketplace has changed,” McClatchy CEO Tony Hunter told staff during the off-the-record Nov. 6 meeting, according to audio provided to Nieman Lab. Executives told staff that McClatchy-owned publications have suffered a 17% decline in paid digital subscribers in the last year — and unique visitors have plummeted 39%.

A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies.

Dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey , McClatchy’s chief operating officer, said at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.”

McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.

Central to the rebrand is the launch of four new websites: Crime Hunter , a site devoted to “real-life crime and justice”; Saltwater South , which “celebrates the places, people and experiences that make the coastal South unlike anywhere else”; Camp & Country , a “national outdoor destination”; and Student Section , billed as “the home of the college sports fan.”

Each of the sites is “powered by Trend Hunter,” a company McClatchy acquired in 2024 that uses AI “to glean insights into consumer trends” and sell consumer goods like $33.91 rosemary oil “to support a healthy scalp environment,” a $249 red light therapy cap to regrow hair “without the hassle of messy serums” and $34.99 “MAGIC Mushroom Coffee” for “clarity, balance and natural energy.”

items.title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite
items.content:
TLDR; We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.

On Kite , our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes.

Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB ( ssdb ), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years.

Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement:

As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were:

So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following:

Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its 35% Faster Than The Filesystem claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates millions of tables every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens?

So we ended up building Blobasaur , an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB.

We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements:

We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves:

SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB.

Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard sqlite3 CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc.

While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust ( sqlx , rusqlite , and tokio ), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary.

In WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly.

items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
items.content:
A screenshot from Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: Rockstar

A screenshot from Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: Rockstar

We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match

After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

W hen I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI .

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that. As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more.

A screenshot from Grand Theft Auto VI. Photograph: Rockstar Sometimes it’s hard to see the impact of these games when you’re working so hard on them. It’s only at times like this that the staggering scale of GTA’s success hits you. GTA V has sold over 230m copies, generating more than $10bn (£7.6bn) in worldwide revenue, surpassing any film in Hollywood’s history. This latest instalment is expected to break those records. Behind these numbers are thousands of people whose talent and hard work make the games possible. With a recognised union, we can ensure everyone, across every department, sees a fair share of the success we contributed to. Our games are industry-leading. Our wages, conditions and bonuses should be too.

While the highs of a game release like this can be incredible, game workers have also come to expect other, less welcome side effects: intense overtime in the buildup and mass redundancies in the aftermath. In previous years, Rockstar has faced allegations of “crunch culture” , where game workers are expected to do unhealthy amounts of overtime in the run-up to a launch. With a strong union we could make sure there is no return to this system. We have already seen the introduction of some overtime pay, and now we want to keep on pushing to ensure that every hour worked in our industry is an hour paid.

After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds. Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years. It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised.

There’s another reason this is a pivotal moment for the UK’s biggest game studio to secure union recognition. The rapid emergence of AI is transforming how studios work and raising fundamental questions about the future of our industry. Across the sector, the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI.…

items.title: Security patch: PHP admins have work to do Thursday afternoon
items.content:
The PHP scripting language is affected by several security issues. Some are rated critical if users deviate from the default settings or use other unusual configurations. All supported PHP versions are affected. PHP hasn’t yet disclosed further details, to give attackers as little time as possible.

PHP will release software updates and technical information Thursday afternoon, between 3 and 3:30 p.m. CET. “Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available‟, the PHP security team emphasizes .

PHP is a widely used scripting language, particularly for building websites. Market watchers estimate that PHP runs on more than two-thirds of all web servers whose server-side programming language is known. Along with the serious security vulnerabilities in the WordPress content management system disclosed Wednesday and those in nginx, the world’s leading web server , this makes for an unsettling security hat trick for web servers.

items.content:
Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 1: A new exploit, which is even worse than this one is currently doing rounds on telegram. Details unknown at this time. Unpatched at the time of writing.

New Instagram Unpatched Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Allegedly, the new method is via Facebook recovery. Apparently, prompting Meta AI to turn on “Development Mode” and attaching proof of account compromise along with email works. More details awaited.

There’s a version of this story where it reads like a hypothetical from a conference talk. An AI agent with elevated backend privileges. A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

A logical flaw in Meta’s AI-powered Instagram account recovery assistant let attackers bypass two-factor authentication entirely not by cracking a code or intercepting an SMS, but by talking the chatbot into doing the work for them. High-value “OG” Instagram handles worth hundreds of thousands of dollars were stolen and resold on Telegram within minutes of each compromise. The dormant Obama White House account got hijacked. Prominent researchers woke up locked out of their own profiles.

items.title: The Bank of Nvidia’s tab jumped to nearly $670 billion — and its customers are taking longer to pay: Chart of the Day
items.content:
The Bank of Nvidia's tab jumped to nearly $670 billion — and its customers are taking longer to pay: Chart of the Day

Wed, November 18, 2026 at 8:00 p.m. GMT+9 3 min read

Jensen Huang started reining in the Bank of Nvidia months before he left. It got bigger anyway.

Third quarter results from Nvidia ( NVDA ) on Tuesday covered the last quarter during which Huang served as CEO. They also updated the number investors have watched since his exit put the company's web of AI deals under the microscope.

Everything Nvidia has promised to buy, back, or invest now comes to nearly $670 billion, up from about $530 billion in July, by Yahoo Finance calculations.

Most of the jump is for chips, not loans. Promises to suppliers swelled to $390 billion from $279 billion, mostly to lock up memory for years to come.

The riskier piece is the backstops. Nvidia carries $118 billion in guarantees — promises to pay if a partner can't — including nearly $10 billion in new ones for partners it didn't name. It says it hasn't paid out on any of them.

"Neoclouds and frontier labs are seeing extraordinary demand for AI infrastructure, yet many are growing faster than their balance sheets and long-term credit profiles can support," interim CEO Colette Kress wrote in her commentary on the quarter .

Nvidia, Yahoo Finance Fewer pledges, same big checks

New pledges did shrink, to $32 billion for neoclouds — cloud companies that rent out Nvidia's chips — and $20 billion for investments in other companies.

But the checks kept coming. Nvidia bought nearly $16 billion of stakes in other companies in the quarter, mostly private ones it didn't name. Among public companies, its latest holdings filing shows it added to SpaceX ( SPCX ) while trimming Intel ( INTC ) and Nokia ( NOK ). So far this fiscal year, those purchases have eaten up nearly half of the cash its business generated, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.

Nvidia, Bank of America, TechCrunch, Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance The IOUs are piling up

Nvidia's accounts receivable — bills sent but not yet paid — hit $81 billion, or 64 days of sales. That's the most since the 2022 chip slump by a measure called days sales outstanding .

Nvidia pointed to "extended payment terms on large, multi-quarter agreements with certain investment-grade customers." In other words, some of its biggest buyers are getting more time to pay.

The full books will have to wait. Nvidia said its 10-Q quarterly report would come "in the coming weeks," not the same evening as usual. Its release also mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.

Nvidia, Yahoo Finance Moat or millstone?

"The deep financing arm of Nvidia is ... a moat that no competitor is ... going to be able to get close to anytime soon," Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy, told Yahoo Finance last week.

Skeptics point to the pandemic-era chip shortage, in which long-term deals didn't protect suppliers once demand slowed. "And then all these long-term supply agreements basically are worthless, right?" Dan Niles of Niles Investment Management told Yahoo Finance Tuesday.

On Tuesday's call, Kress signaled the bank may be choosier from here. "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees," she said.

items.title: LLM assisted reverse engineering
items.content:
I have been hacking both hardware and software for 2 decades. Previously manually. But in 2026 with the help of AIs the proccess is greatly sped up. Below I will describe my proccess briefly or how I do it.

Thats the AI I am using. Occasionaly I use Codex with Luna or Terra but Deepseek is super performant, fast and cheap

The best in the market, free, disassembler and decompiler. With the MCP bridge agents can use it very well

CLI disassemblers and decompilers. Not as good as Ghidra but much faster and possibly better usable for AIs

What I basically do nowadays is just point the agent at the binary to be analysed and use my set of dedicated agent skills. Rest usually takes care of itself. But putting the skills besides, the flow is basically this.

Find binary type, platform, build etc - based on this using appropriate decompiler (note - current AIs do fairly well with just disassembly . ie pure x86 or ARM instructions).

Command agent to document all findings along the way to MD files. This serves several purposes. They become notes for your own understanding. They help the agent not lose the track after compaction / handoff to different agent. And last but not least, it helps the agent work more effectively, not get lost in circles etc. More about this later.

Ask the agent to analyse basic structure. Main functions, main branching, imported functions etc of given binary. By binary I mean whatever. Desktop executable, website or firmware image.

Once I have this basic overview I can usually proceed any way I need to do modifications to the original binary or build mods or just help me understand it better.

On some occasions some things are not easily resolvable by simple disassembly or decompilation. In those cases you can do:

Let the agent debug given binary and set breakpoints on specific parts to help it figure out given inner workings.

Use logging. Either by somehow enabling it in the original binary or by making a probe (and this can mean many things) that injects to the original binary and records you via logs (to file) whatever is needed to resolve given feature.

Give agent outside access - ie computer use for desktop apps, or api controllable emulator for running and controlling given firmware.

Ask agent to try different approach. But you must be specific. Ie when it gets stuck in disasembly by following xrefs, ask it to try to follow strings in the binary instead.

Read the entire LLM conversation and thinking. Current LLMs are smart but they still sometimes get to a narrow approach. By reading the traces you can often instinctively figure the agent it going into a blind path and give it suggestion as to how it might be approached better. That however skill of your own to have.

Here are some of my major skills I use frequently.

It gives you several questions when your input might be valuable. I usually use it with this prompt:

whose answers are crucial for your further progress.

mattpocock / skills Shell Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab.

It helps a ton to have a skill where your specific reverse engineering tooling is described. Ie to use radare2 or kuna. Or description of how to use the MCP Ghidra bridge and for what. Without such a skill, agents often give up too quickly getting lost, not knowing how to do the actual disassembly / decompilation.

items.title: Solid 2.0
items.content:
5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then. A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler. More recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time. If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design. This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands: const user = createMemo (() => fetchUser (props.id)); < h1 class = {{ stale : isPending (user) }} > { user ().name} fetchUser(props.id)); return ( }>

{user().name}

  );}"> This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth. SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below. import { live } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions" ; const stockPrice = live ( async function* ( symbol : string ) { for await ( const tick of subscribe (symbol)) yield tick.price; const price = createMemo (() => stockPrice ()) This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability. "But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in. Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong. In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will update. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix: [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] Reactive value read directly in an effect callback will not update. Move it into a tracking scope (JSX, a memo, or an effect's compute function). at http://localhost:5173/src/Item.tsx:12:19 [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] what it means and how to fix it:…

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: GTA 6 Hacker Faces Jail as Crypto Thief Gets 6 Years
items.content:

A GTA 6 hacker from Oxford has admitted his part in a string of major cyberattacks, while a second British hacker has just received a six-year prison term in the United States for stealing millions in cryptocurrency. Both men belonged to the same loose network of young cybercriminals, and their cases land in the same week that Grand Theft Auto 6 reaches players .

Arion Kurtaj, 21, of Oxford, pleaded guilty on 16 November to hacking Rockstar Games, Uber, Revolut and BT

Tyler Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, got 72 months (six years) in a US federal prison on 17 November

Buchanan’s phishing scheme stole more than $11.6 million in cryptocurrency

Both men belonged to the Lapsus$ and Scattered Spider hacking circles

Kurtaj’s sentencing date is still unannounced, and Buchanan’s restitution hearing is set for 11 December

GTA 6 Hacker Arion Kurtaj Admits Guilt in London Court

Arion Kurtaj, now 21, entered his guilty pleas at Woolwich Crown Court in London on 16 November. The charges cover several attacks he carried out as a teenager. They include the break-in at Rockstar Games, the studio behind the Grand Theft Auto series, plus attacks on Uber, the digital bank Revolut and the phone company BT.

The Rockstar breach exposed 90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 footage, roughly 60 minutes of gameplay in total. Rockstar has said the leak cost it about $5 million in recovery work. Prosecutors have not yet announced a sentencing date, so the length of his punishment remains unknown.

How the GTA 6 Hacker Broke In From a Hotel Room

The story behind the Rockstar hack reads like a heist film. Police had already seized Kurtaj’s laptop and placed him in a hotel in Bicester, Oxfordshire, to protect him from rival criminal gangs. He still managed to break into the studio’s internal systems with an Amazon Fire TV stick, the hotel television and a mobile phone. Authorities say those attacks broke his bail conditions.

Once inside, he announced himself in the company’s team chat as an outside attacker and demanded that Rockstar contact him on Telegram or face a public data dump. He followed through and posted the stolen clips online. The leak gave fans their first look at the game more than a year before the official trailer arrived, and early footage pointed to a Vice City setting with the series’ first female lead.

From Hospital Order to Guilty Plea: The Kurtaj Timeline

2022: Kurtaj hacks Rockstar Games and leaks the GTA 6 footage while living under police protection.

December 2023: A UK court finds him responsible for the attacks but rules him unfit to stand trial, citing his autism diagnosis and the high risk he would return to hacking. The judge orders indefinite detention in a secure hospital.

2026: Kurtaj leaves the hospital unit and moves to prison to await a fresh criminal case.

16 November 2026: He pleads guilty to the Rockstar, Uber, Revolut and BT attacks.

Crypto Thief Tyler Buchanan Gets Six Years in US Prison

On the other side of the Atlantic, a federal court in Santa Ana, California, sentenced Tyler Buchanan to six years on Tuesday, 17 November. The 24-year-old from Dundee, Scotland, pleaded guilty in April 2026 to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, and he faced a maximum of 22 years. Spanish police arrested him in June 2024, the United States charged him that November, and he has sat in US custody since his extradition in April 2025.

Prosecutors say the scheme ran from 2021 to 2023 and drained more than $11.6 million in cryptocurrency from victims across the country. The largest single theft, in December 2022, cost one victim about $1.67 million. A restitution hearing on 11 December will decide how much Buchanan and his co-defendants must repay.
